title: Find the Duplicate Number: Floyd's on index→value mapping.
shortTitle: Find the Duplicate Number: Floyd's on Index-to-Value Mapping
keyPoints: Treat each value as a pointer to the next index; the duplicate creates a cycle in this functional graph.
Floyd's two-phase algorithm finds the cycle entry, which is the duplicated value, in O(n) time and O(1) space.
Phase one: slow moves one step, fast moves two steps, until they meet inside the cycle.
Phase two: reset one pointer to start, advance both by one step until they meet at the cycle entry.
This is the only approach that satisfies both read-only array and constant-space constraints.
Alternatives: sorting mutates the array, a HashSet uses O(n) space, and binary search on value range is O(n log n).

s1_definition.oneliner: Follow values as next-index pointers; the duplicate creates a cycle, and Floyd's algorithm finds the cycle's entry, which is the duplicate.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Problem** – given an array of n+1 integers where every value is between 1 and n, exactly one value is duplicated; find it without modifying the array and using O(1) space.
- **Key insight** – treat each value as a pointer to the next index, forming a functional graph with a guaranteed cycle.
- **Floyd's algorithm** – a two-phase cycle detection: phase one finds a meeting point inside the cycle, phase two finds the cycle entry.
- **Cycle entry** – the index where two different positions point to, which is the duplicated value.
- **Constraints** – read-only array and constant extra space rule out sorting, HashSet, and negation tricks.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a list of branch codes where one code was accidentally entered twice, and the array is read-only because other services reference it. Rajesh treats each slot's value as an arrow pointing to another slot. Because the duplicate makes two arrows land on the same slot, the arrows form a loop. The slot where the loop begins is the repeated code, and Floyd's tortoise-and-hare finds it without touching the array.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Find the Duplicate Number gives me an array of n plus one integers whose values all lie between 1 and n, with exactly one value repeated, and asks me to find that value without modifying the array and in constant space. The key trick is to treat each value as a pointer to the next index, forming a functional graph. Because two different indices point to the same next index, the graph contains a cycle, and the entry node of that cycle is the duplicated value.

That reframing lets me use Floyd's two-phase cycle detection. In phase one I advance a slow pointer by one hop and a fast pointer by two hops through this value-as-index mapping until they meet inside the cycle. In phase two I reset one pointer to the start and advance both by a single hop until they meet again, and the position where they converge is the duplicate.

The reason I reach for this specific method is the pair of constraints. Sorting would modify the array, a HashSet would use O(n) space, and the negation trick mutates the input, so all three are disallowed. Floyd's is the one approach that satisfies both read-only and constant-space constraints. Starting the pointers from `nums[0]` avoids the self-loop at index 0.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India, I used this in the routing-code validation service. A read-only array of branch routing codes had exactly one code duplicated by a data-entry error, and the service had to identify it without altering the shared array. Floyd's cycle detection found the duplicate in linear time and constant space.

Remember one sentence: treat values as next-index pointers, detect the cycle with Floyd's tortoise and hare, and the cycle entry is the duplicate.
